_note: Batch: The Christian Recorder (Philadelphia; weekly/semi-monthly organ of the A.M.E. Church, published by the Book Committee; Rev. J. P. Campbell, editor, office Lombard St., Philadelphia) -- pilot from the 1854-56 microfilm reel, PDF cr1856.pdf (5 two-page spreads). IMPORTANT DISCOVERY: the five spreads contain TWO issues, not one. Newspaper pages 1-4 are Vol. I, No. 38, Friday, January 18, 1856 (No. 38 and the Jan. 18 date verified on the page-1 masthead and page-2 editorial head). Pages 5-8 are Vol. I, No. 39, Tuesday, March 4, 1856 (running pages 150-155; date verified on the p6 editorial head 'TUESDAY, MARCH 4, 1856' and consistent with internal dates -- Zanesville letter of Jan. 31, Wayman letter of Jan. 26, and the Richard Allen anniversary of February; the paper evidently missed its biweekly schedule between Nos. 38 and 39). Per the caller's instruction all records below carry the single slug CR_1856-01-18 with the physical page numbers 1-8 of this OCR set; records on pages 5-8 belong to the March 4 issue and say so in their text. Extraction rule per Michiko (Philadelphia-focused, as for the Colored American): deep-read Philadelphia AME affairs, meetings, notices, signed letters, ads with proprietors and addresses; skim reprint/devotional matter (p4 'Indigestion' from Budd on the Stomach and 'Fashion'; p8 Moravian Jamaica letter and poetry) while noting named AME clergy anywhere. OCR was column-by-column from microfilm and noisy; every signature, officer, and address below was verified against 400-dpi page-image crops. Key OCR rescues: 'Titos Newnise' = THOS. SUNRISE (the Oneida Indian preacher received into the New England Conference); 'J.C. Besta/C. Bean' = J. C. BEMAN; 'Vorcarren' = PRESBYTER (pseudonym); 'J.P. Tvosen/Joseph Petuasen/Towmen' = J. P. TURNER / JOSEPH P. TURNER of New Bedford (three letters); 'A. R. Carty' = A. R. GREEN; 'Srernen Sorru' = STEPHEN SMITH, Local Elder; 'James A. orter' = JAMES A. SHORTER; 'Deuton Dorre' = Rev. DENTON DORREL (first name could read Deuton); 'Mrs. Ravan, 259 Lombard' = MRS. ROYAL, 252 Lombard; 'jeua WEAVER' = ELISHA WEAVER; 'A.Kixr/A.Key' = A. KENT; 'J. DL. Brown' = J. M. BROWN; 'Rev. Mr. Tamer' = Rev. Mr. TURNER; 'I. OU. Youeg' = Rev. H. C. YOUNG; 'Wenghty' = Mr. WAUGHTY. Still uncertain after image checks: Rev. William Mook (speaker at the Allen anniversary -- possibly Monk or Moore); Kinnard's street number 390 vs 300 Cherry; 'U. A. Widal's, 303 Lombard' (almost certainly Ulysses A. Vidal); Mrs. J. B. Smith's Providence street (reads Wilmington, possibly Washington); Rev. Peter Gardener/Gardiner; amount of Wm. M. Watson's payment ($10 or $15); the Allen anniversary date printed 'Thursday, 4th of February' though Feb. 4, 1856 was a Monday (Feb. 14 was the Thursday). Pages with no qualifying content beyond skim: p4 (medical reprint 'Indigestion' from Budd on the Stomach, published by Blanchard & Lea, Philada., and 'Fashion -- What She Does'); p8 (Moravian Jamaica letter of J. H. Buchner, Moravian mission statistics, poetry, James Montgomery verses, California crime squib). [Post-pilot split 2026-08-19: pages 5-8 were Vol I No. 39, Tuesday 1856-03-04 -- those records now carry slug CR_1856-03-04 with pages renumbered 1-4; the shared source PDF holds both issues.]

articles.headline: Committee on Episcopacy, Increase of Bishops, etc., etc.
articles.author: Presbyter (pseudonym), Mount Pisgah, Jan. 1st, 1856
articles.summary: 'Editor Campbell:--Reading over the last number of your paper, my attention was particularly attracted by a communication over the signature of W. M., which I regard as being a very important one. I refer to what he says about a committee on the episcopacy.' The writer agrees the Bishops should undergo an examination at every General Conference (though before the whole body, not a committee), favours an increase of Bishops -- 'Give us a Bishop for every district, who can properly represent the connexion' -- provided men of literary as well as Christian dignity can be found, and proposes amending the Discipline so that the assistant whom a Bishop chooses to sit with him shall not be eligible for election as Bishop at the ensuing General Conference, lest the office become 'an hereditary one.' Signed 'Yours as ever, Presbyter' (signature verified from the page image; OCR gave 'Vorcarren').

articles.headline: The Efficacy of Prayer
articles.author: J. C. Beman, Middletown, Connecticut, Dec. 19, 1855
articles.summary: 'Mr. Editor--Dear Sir, allow me a small space in your valuable Recorder. I have been thinking on prayer...' An essay on why ministers need the prayers of the church, from 2 Thess. iii. 1, citing Paul and Silas at Thessalonica, Aaron and Hur, and Wesley on preaching; 'how much easier to preach to a praying Church... So prays one who is less than the least of all saints.' Signed J. C. Beman (signature verified from the page image; this is Jehiel C. Beman, the Middletown A.M.E. Zion/temperance leader as printed, recorded here exactly as signed).

articles.headline: Answer on receiving ministers from other denominations
articles.author: Thos. Sunrise
articles.summary: 'Mr. Editor.--The following is an answer, with preliminary remarks, to the question... in the Recorder dated No. 3[6]... Ought ministers to be received from other denominations into our conferences, and stationed preachers in charge over us, who themselves have never been members of our church?' The writer shows the A.M.E. Discipline (like the old M.E. Discipline) provides for receiving ministers from other evangelical denominations 'according to our usages,' and gives his own case: the New England Annual Conference, held in Providence, R.I., June 16th, received him for two years' probation and appointed him a missionary, giving him only five dollars for his year's support -- proof he did not come 'for the loaves and fishes.' Some seven or eight years before he had applied to join under the charge of Thomas Lawrence, in Pittsburgh, Pa., and was refused because the constitution then did not allow receiving persons 'unless they were descendants of Africans': 'I am not of African descent... I have seen the rights, privileges, and happiness taken from the oppressed Ethiopians; and when I looked around and seen the oppression, affliction, and deplorable condition of the Indians, I came to the conclusion that we are both fellow sufferers.' Signed 'Yours, fraternally, Thos. Sunrise' (verified from the image; the Oneida Indian preacher), with a P.S. on his subscription signed T. S. and an editorial reply ('Brother Sunrise will learn from the Christian Recorder, published just after the sitting of the New England Conference... Editor.') on page 1, column 4.

articles.headline: On Increasing the Number of Bishops, with the Editor's Remarks
articles.author: W. N.
articles.summary: '(For the Christian Recorder.) Mr. Editor.--As I see so many contemplated plans at our next General Conference... let them examine the following questions: First, is the membership increasing or decreasing in our churches? Second, will the contemplated increase of high functionaries in the church increase its harmony and peace, or bring about more of a sectional feeling...? Third, are the means of support more abundant...?' Signed W. N. The Editor follows with 'Remarks on the questions proposed by W. N.,' answering that in some churches membership is decreasing but in others certainly increasing (referring to the published minutes of the several Annual Conferences), that bishops in each district would increase harmony, and that means of support increase with the efficiency of the ministry; signed Editor. A 'Scraps' column of foreign religious items closes the page.

articles.headline: Members of the General Conference (editorial)
articles.author: Rev. J. P. Campbell, Editor
articles.summary: 'The next General Conference, according to the existing rule, will be composed of all travelling preachers whose character and standing are fair, and who have travelled four full years next preceding its sitting; and one delegate, a four years regularly licensed local preacher or minister, for every six hundred lay members...' The editor argues this representation 'is vastly too large for all practical purposes' and proposes about one travelling delegate for every ten members of each annual conference and an equal number of local delegates, elected by regular ballotings upon a call of the roll; by such an arrangement the General Conference of 1860, four years hence, would consist of from forty-five to sixty members -- enough 'to transact the business of a General Conference for thirty thousand members.' (This is the editorial to which Stephen Smith replies in the March 4 issue, page 5 of this set.) Recovered largely from the page image; the OCR of this column failed.

articles.headline: Review of Brother Wears' article on Presiding Elders (editorial; heading partly illegible)
articles.author: Rev. J. P. Campbell, Editor
articles.summary: An editorial reviewing an article by 'Brother Wears' -- a man 'of more than ordinary mind, and gifted with extraordinary talent' whose 'more than ordinary high-toned moral and religious rectitude' the editor also attests -- which had favoured creating the order of Presiding Elders in the A.M.E. Church. The editor recalls his earlier reply to Rev. J. M. Brown, 'who in the thirty-fourth number of the Christian Recorder suggested the creation of the office of Presiding Elder as it is found in the Methodist Episcopal Church in America and in the British Wesleyan Conference,' agrees with Wears on ministerial failures and the need to support preachers whose wives and children want bread and clothes, but opposes any new order -- 'if white men have Arch-Bishops, Cardinals, and Popes, our people will be sure to want them' -- and argues instead for increasing the number of Bishops: 'We want a Bishop for each and every District.' (The Wears under review is not further identified in print; Philadelphia's Isaiah C. Wears is the likely man but the paper prints only 'Bro. Wears.')

articles.headline: Queries upon the Subject of Receiving Ministers from Other Denominations
articles.author: Editorial
articles.summary: Editorial catechism on the question raised in the thirty-sixth number ('A serious question to be settled by the A.M.E. Church'): whether ministers from other denominations must become members of the A.M.E. Church, pass through its offices, and graduate through the Quarterly Conference before taking charge. Four questions are answered, holding membership and practical acquaintance with the government, doctrine and discipline an invariable pre-requisite, since a minister among us is 'at one and the same time, a legislator, a judge, and a governor.'

articles.headline: Governmental Reform
articles.author: W. Moore
articles.summary: 'Mr. Editor.--I wish now to call the attention of the Brethren to the present state of things in our Society. You are aware that our fathers, when they braved the storm for religious liberty, established a church founded on Apostolic principles...' A call to return to the general rules and discipline of early Methodism: 'It has become quite fashionable among us for our brethren to do as they please... Let the fountain be pure and the stream will be pure also. Yours most respectfully in favour of a general reformation in the Church. W. Moore.' (Begins on page 2, column 4; signature verified from the page image.)

articles.headline: Against adding bishops or the presiding eldership (letter beginning 'Is it logical, if a ship is about to sink...')
articles.author: J. P. Turner, New Bedford, Dec. 20th, 1855
articles.summary: 'Mr. Editor--Is it logical, if a ship is about to sink under one ton burden, for those who may be interested to add another ton to prevent the catastrophe?' The connexion is already sinking under the support of the Book Concern, the superannuated preachers' fund, the missions, the Sabbath-school enterprise, and the general superintendency; the brethren who want to add 'thirty-three bishops, or the presiding eldership, as it is turned out to be... it is the same rabbit that leaped out of the bush,' must be resisted -- 'if I am a man that troubles Israel, as my soul liveth, I will not leave yet; for I, like Sampson, hope to slay more at the end than I have done in all the days of my life.' He concurs with the suggestion (in the last number) that an elder should also have power to put a steward in the chair when compelled to bring a charge against one of his members, and pleads for 'freedom of speech, religiously and also politically.' Signature J. P. Turner verified from the page image (OCR gave 'J.P. Tvosen').

articles.headline: On the Unity of the Church
articles.author: Joseph P. Turner, New Bedford, Dec. 29th, 1855
articles.summary: 'Mr. Editor,--Sir, having in your last number, we hear, a voice for union in the A.M.E. Church, I will take the liberty of commenting on the subject.' Are we not all under one general superintendency, one common brotherhood? Are our bishops equal and co-equal? 'Cannot one Bishop right a wrong in one part of the connexion as well as another?... let us meet every brother upon a level on our conference floors,' with the exception that a brother belonging to another conference appearing as counsel in a case of trial shall not vote on a district matter -- 'and then we will not let the mere value of dollars and cents separate us... Yours, for union in the A.M.E. Church, Joseph P. Turner.' (Signature verified from the page image; OCR gave 'Towmen.')

articles.headline: Bishop Nazrey's Plan for Creating a Fund toward the Support of the Book Concern (a concurring letter)
articles.author: Joseph P. Turner, New Bedford, Dec. 11th, 1855
articles.summary: 'Mr. Editor,--Dear sir, I fully concur with the plan suggested for the support of the Book Concern, with some little addition, viz: three dollars a year for the support of the minister -- and his salary, making a total of four dollars and fifty cents per year, and that to be paid weekly,' the payment to be a requisite of good membership with all its rights and privileges (the sacrament, bringing charges, admittance to love feast, form of trial), on neglect of which members shall be liable to be dropped as probationers. Answering the objection that in large cities this would overpay the minister, he would put the overplus into a fund for ministers labouring where the people cannot support them: 'let the strong bear the infirmities of the weak.' Ministers who teach a people contrary to this through false sympathy should be dealt with as teaching false doctrine; badly supported ministers are one reason 'our ministry have made so little progress in literature.' Signed (page image) '...P. Turner, New Bedford, Dec. 11th, 1855.'

articles.headline: Bishop's Notices of the Philadelphia and New England District Annual Conferences, and Notice from Bishop Nazrey to Preachers in Charge
articles.author: Bishop Willis Nazrey, Chatham, C.W.
articles.summary: The Philadelphia District Annual Conference will meet on the last Saturday, or 31st day of May, 1856, at 9 o'clock, in the A.M.E. Bethel Church, on Sixth street, below Pine street, Philadelphia; punctual attendance of the members is requested. Also, the New England District Annual Conference will meet in the city of Boston, Mass., the 21st day of June, 1856, at 9 o'clock; each elder in charge will notify the delegates. Each district will strictly attend to their financial duties as usual. All persons wishing to communicate with Bishop Nazrey must direct their letters, post-paid, to Chatham, C.W. [Canada West], until the middle of the month of April. A second notice directs the preachers in charge of circuits and stations in the Philadelphia and New England districts to notify the delegates to the General Conference elected at the time and place appointed, in accordance with the discipline, page 62, paragraph 3d, and explains section 7th, page 23 (much inquired of), as intended to collect means to send the delegates out and bring them home again, those near the seat of the conference bearing the incidental expenses. Both signed Willis Nazrey.

articles.headline: Notice to Those Pledging Donations for the Support of the Christian Recorder
articles.author: The Editor and General Book Steward (Rev. J. P. Campbell)
articles.summary: 'We do hereby request those brethren who subscribed their names, in the Philadelphia and New England Annual Conferences, to pay the sum of ten dollars towards the support of the Christian Recorder for one year, upon the plan of Rev. Peter Gardener [Gardiner], to forward the same, or at least a goodly portion of it, to the Book Committee, as we are now in immediate want of it... Brethren, shall the Christian Recorder live, or shall it die? Be pleased to answer this question.' (The notice is repeated verbatim on page 5, in the March 4 issue.)

articles.headline: The Lord's Free-will Offering
articles.author: Book Committee / Editor
articles.summary: The Lord's Free-will Offering was a donation asked for by the Book Committee at the celebration of the act of incorporation of the Book Concern; a number of ministers responded 'most nobly,' but whole Conferences have passed us by: 'New York Conference barely escaped, by the generous heart of Rev. Denton Dorrel, of Newark, N.J. Ohio, Indiana, Canada, and Missouri Conferences, have done nothing. Brethren, come over and help us.' (Name verified against the image; the first name prints as Denton or Deuton Dorrel.)

articles.headline: Donation to the Christian Recorder, and Monies received to this date
articles.author: Editor
articles.summary: 'Rev. James A. Shorter, elder in charge of Ebenezer Church, Baltimore, Md., has forwarded us the sum of $10.00, toward the support of the Christian Recorder, until we meet in the general Conference. Brothers in the ministry, will you, in the name of the Lord, do likewise?... Monies received to this date: Rev. Wm. M. Watson, on account, $1[0?].00 (amount partly illegible, $10 or $15); Brother Jeremiah Young, on account, $3.00; Rev. J. A. Shorter, donation to the Christian Recorder, $10.00.' All names verified against the page image.

articles.headline: Notice -- Hope Grand Union, No. 1, D. of T., State of Pennsylvania
articles.author: Officers of the Hope Grand Union
articles.summary: 'Hope Grand Union, No. 1, D. of T. [Daughters of Temperance], State of Pennsylvania, are still prepared to open Unions, and grant Charters, throughout the United States. All communications may be addressed: Mrs. Bundy, G.P.P.S., No. 356 South street, above Eighth; Mrs. Hall, G.P.S., No. 5 Buckley street; or, Mrs. Royal, G.S., No. 252 Lombard street, Philadelphia.' All three officers' names and addresses verified from the page image (OCR had corrupted 'Royal, 252' to 'Ravan, 259').

articles.headline: Boarding House
articles.author: Mrs. J. B. Smith, Providence, R.I.
articles.summary: 'Mrs. J. B. Smith takes pleasure in announcing to the travelling public, that she has opened a commodious BOARDING HOUSE at No. 133 Wilmington Street, Providence, R.I.' -- 'one of the most pleasant, healthy and recreative situations in the city.' Address Rev. J. B. Smith, Providence, Rhode Island. (Street name reads Wilmington on the image; possibly Washington -- microfilm blur.)

articles.headline: Business notices and advertisements (page 3 / running page 151)
articles.author: Various proprietors
articles.summary: (1) Dr. Litch's Restorative and Dr. Litch's Pain Curer, 'Sold at 203 Lombard Street' -- cures for colds, coughs, scrofulous tumours and sores, rheumatism, colic, etc., 25 and 50 cents; testimonial: ''I have used Dr. Litch's Restorative, and Pain Curer, and can heartily recommend them for family medicines. WM. STILL.'' Sold by Dr. Litch, Eleventh and Cherry, and Mrs. H. Deuteste, South, below Ninth Street, and by druggists. (2) J. J. GOULD BIAS, M.D., Reformed Eclectic MEDICINE STORE, No. 393 Federal Street, one door above Twelfth -- North side (office back), Philadelphia; office hours 7 to 9 A.M., 2 to 3 and 6 to 8 P.M.; herbs and roots of all kinds constantly on hand. (3) 'FIRE! FIRE!! FIRE!!!' -- Superior WHITE ASH COAL at the Coal and Lumber Yard, corner of Broad and Willow streets, kept dry under cover at the lowest cash prices -- SMITH, WHIPPER & CO. [Stephen Smith and William Whipper]; orders may be left at the Book-store of the A. Meth. Ep. Church, Lombard street, below Sixth, and at U. A. Widal's [almost certainly Ulysses A. Vidal], 303 Lombard street; dated Philadelphia, Jan. 26, 1855. (4) 'HATS! HATS!!' -- P. A. Brown's Spring and Summer style of hats cannot be surpassed; Hat and Cap Store, No. 198 South Sixth Street, above Lombard -- opposite Bethel Church; dated Philadelphia, May 28, 1855. (5) 'Our World' ('For Truth, our Country, and the Slave'), 603 pages, 10 illustrations, $1.25, on the Great Question of slavery, 'superior to Uncle Tom's Cabin' (Buffalo Express); Miller, Orton & Co., Publishers, 25 Park Row, New York, and 107 Genesee street, Auburn. (6) THOMAS M. KINNARD, SURGEON DENTIST, No. 390 [digit unclear, possibly 300] Cherry Street, above Thirteenth, Philadelphia -- toothache cured, teeth filled with pure gold, artificial teeth, extraction without pain, difficult surgical cases attended to; 'Thos. M. Kinnard would strongly urge the attention of parents and guardians... having all irregularities of the teeth of young persons promptly attended to. Terms moderate.' (7) 'Is Sebastopol Armageddon?' -- pamphlet of historical facts calculated to prove that Sebastopol is Armageddon, views similar to the celebrated Dr. Cumming; price 10 cents; address C. MYERS, Publisher, care of W. S. Young, 50 North Sixth St., Phila. The same Bias, Smith Whipper & Co., Brown, Our World, and Kinnard advertisements are repeated on page 7 (running page 155) of the March 4 issue.

articles.headline: Indigestion (from 'Budd on the Stomach') and Fashion -- What She Does
articles.author: None (selected matter)
articles.summary: 'All writers on indigestion, from the time of Celsus, have laid down general rules or maxims...' A long popular-medicine selection on mastication, meals and drinks, credited 'Selected from Budd on the Stomach, recently published by Messrs. Blanchard & Lea, Philada.'; followed by the moral squib 'Fashion -- what she does.' No local names; page skimmed per rule.

articles.headline: Letter from Zanesville, Ohio: revival at the second quarterly meeting
articles.author: A. R. Green, Zanesville, Jan. 31, 1856
articles.summary: 'The Lord is reviving his work in a powerful manner in this my appointment.' An account of the revival that followed the second quarterly meeting of Jan. 13th (see events). In a postscript Green reviews the Recorder's correspondence on reforms in the Discipline: he concurs with the correspondent 'Itinerant' on the bishop's council, and 'most heartily joins hands with W. M., No. 37, in his Proposed Committee on the Episcopacy,' one that will examine closely the acts and deeds, both in travelling and administration of discipline. Signed A. R. Green (verified from the page image; OCR gave 'A. R. Carty').

articles.headline: On the reception of ministers from other denominations: the law, the usage, and where the blame rests
articles.author: A. R. G. [A. R. Green]
articles.summary: A long reply to the editor's 'Serious Question to be Settled by the African Methodist Episcopal Church' (No. 36) on receiving ministers from other denominations, quoting Matt. xvii. 24-27 and the revised Discipline (pages 84, 86, 94, 102-103): the law of reception 'is as good as we can make, if it is only adhered to and practiced,' and 'the burden of responsibility is with the bishops and conferences.' He gives two contrasting cases from his own conference: a brother who came from another denomination in 1853, took the ordination vows before the bishop without any recommendation from a quarterly conference, and -- over the writer's protest as secretary of the conference, for which a visiting bishop administered 'a most scathing rebuke' in 1854 -- was in 1855 pronounced a member of the Annual Conference without examination, recommendation, or vote; while another brother, a converted, reared-up class-leader, trustee, steward, exhorter, local preacher, deacon, elder 'and even sexton' of our connexion and a regular member of the Baltimore Annual Conference, was refused admission until the bishop of the B. district, being present, formally recommended him -- 'and by the by, both cases were from the same station and church.' He proposes that applicants make themselves known to the preacher in charge at least three months before the annual conference and pass their character in the quarterly conference. Signed A. R. G. (signature verified from the page image).

articles.headline: 'Strike! but hear' -- reply to the editorial on the members of the General Conference
articles.author: Stephen Smith, Local Elder
articles.summary: 'Mr. Editor:--Strike! but hear, uttered the philosopher and sage... Now, Mr. Editor, your article of the 18th instant, in reference to the members of the general conference, is in violation of those maxims of philosophy, legislation, and religion I have quoted.' Smith charges that the editor not only impeaches the wisdom and goodness of the General Conference's own rule of representation as unsuited to the wants of the church, but invites discussion calculated to produce disaffection without a fair opportunity to test the law: 'I have hitherto regarded the Christian Recorder as the organ of our church... It has been regarded as the special duty of the Editor to build up, not tear down. It is the province of correspondents to suggest alterations, and the Editor's to examine, explain, and defend the existing order of things. I, therefore, will not accept your invitation to discuss the subject... I am law abiding. I remain yours for the union, peace and stability of the A.M.E. church, Stephen Smith, Local Elder.' (This is the Philadelphia lumber merchant and local elder Stephen Smith, replying to Campbell's Jan. 18 editorial on page 2 of this set.)

articles.headline: The Presiding Eldership (editorial)
articles.author: Rev. J. P. Campbell, Editor
articles.summary: 'Three classes of persons ask for the creation of Presiding Elders': those who would relieve the Bishops by a substitute clothed with episcopal authority; office-seekers; and members who want 'a master over' the preacher in charge, 'someone before whom they may bring him up and have him tried' -- persons who 'like the troubled sea are continually casting up mire and dirt... the continual troublers of Israel.' The editor declares himself 'most heartily opposed' to the office on account of its inutility, oppressive designs and wickedness in practical development, 'as seen in the history of the church from which the idea is a borrowed one.'

articles.headline: Right Rev. Richard Allen (anniversary at Bethel Church)
articles.author: By a Spectator
articles.summary: 'At an anniversary held in Bethel Church on Thursday, 4th of February, to celebrate the life and death of the Rt. Rev. Richard Allen, formerly Bishop of the said Church, the following is an extract of the proceedings.' Report of the Philadelphia commemoration (see events for the full proceedings and speakers), closing: 'Will the Rev. J. P. Campbell let us see his reasons for not being present according to promise?'

articles.headline: Presiding Elder Question Not Settled
articles.author: J. M. Brown
articles.summary: 'Mr. Editor,--Your publication of the communication, addressed to Rev. A. C. Crippin in July, has been the occasion of two editorials reviewing it on the idea advanced in it, viz: That the office of Presiding Elder is necessary to meet the present and improved state of our Church.' Brown answers the editor's objections as 'dust... cast into the people's as well as some of the preachers' eyes': the question is not whether it will cost the East $7,500 per annum; the true issue is whether the church will leave members without a court of appeal or a judge to preside in it. He presses the hardship of appeals to the Annual Conference on a member in New Orleans, La., or San Francisco (fifteen hundred or five thousand miles), and on enslaved members: 'suppose the brother or sister happens to be a slave... Can they leave their homes to meet the annual meeting of the ministers? Or are these members an exception to your rule, and their rights less sacred than others?' 'Preachers and people are suffering from bad administration from almost one end of the connexion to the other. The remedy is all we seek... We do not, as has been intimated in the weakness of a good brother, seek the disunion of the connexion. As ever yours, &c., J. M. Brown.' (Signature verified from the page image.)

articles.headline: Getting the eastern delegates to the General Conference (letter from Baltimore)
articles.author: A. W. Wayman, Baltimore, January 26, 1856
articles.summary: 'To Rev. J. P. Campbell--The time is approaching when the eleventh General Conference of the A.M.E. Church will sit in the Queen city [Cincinnati]. I have not seen as yet any plan suggested by which we may all meet at some point, and start for the conference. I think in 1844 there was a perfect understanding with all the eastern members where to meet.' Wayman asks for information through the Recorder so the entire eastern membership can secure a cheap passage; the members and delegates of the Baltimore district are anxious to know the cost. He also hopes the general conference will lessen the number of delegates (some brethren are absent from their charges one to two months), and, whether the church adds bishops or presiding elders, wants one thing done away with among Christian ministers: 'that unhallowed practice of caucusing... Instead of caucusing make it a subject of prayer. A. W. Wayman.' An editorial note adds: 'Brother Wayman will hear from us in next number.--Ed.'

articles.headline: The Necessity of Union between the Itinerancy and Locality of the Ministry in the A.M.E. Church
articles.author: W. D. W. Schureman
articles.summary: 'Brother Campbell:--It is high time that we as ministers were awake to the interests of our church. We that stand as watchmen on the walls of Zion, should see eye to eye... Sir, it is a lamentable truth, the itinerancy and locality of our church are much disunited.' Using the four beasts full of eyes of Revelation iv. 6, the eyes before representing the itinerant and the eyes behind the local ministry, Schureman pleads that the local brethren watched 'with a godly eye over the affairs of the church' from the apostles' days, laments the busybodies of both classes who disgrace the annual conferences, and urges that this young Conference [the New Jersey district], 'having its birth' recently, be kept clear of such matters. (Byline 'By W. D. W. Schureman' verified from the page image; continues onto page 7.)

articles.headline: What is Justifying Faith?
articles.author: A. Kent, New Bedford, December 29th, 1855
articles.summary: 'Rev. J. P. Campbell:--This is an important question which has caused much controversy among men. When Mr. Wesley became an advocate for the doctrine of justification by faith, it awoke alarming fears throughout the English church.' Quoting the June 1744 conference question 'What is faith?' and Wesley's Works, vol. V, on justifying faith as 'a divine, supernatural evidence or conviction... that Christ died for my sins, that he loved me, and gave himself for me,' the writer regrets the framers of the A.M.E. discipline did not publish Wesley's clearer definition, and suggests the approaching general conference 'think on this subject, and see if there may not be some change for the better.' (Signed A. Ke[nt] -- final letters blurred on the film; same New Bedford writer as the Presiding Eldership letter below.)

articles.headline: Dedication (of the A.M.E. church in Chicago)
articles.author: Elisha Weaver
articles.summary: 'Brother Campbell:--I sat down on purpose to address to you a short communication in relation to the dedication of our church here in Chicago...' Full particulars of the January 6, 1856 dedication (see events): procession up the aisle reading the 84th Psalm, the consecration hymn from the Lute of Zion, the bishop's sermon from the 27th Psalm, 'a crowded house, good order and decorum,' one hundred and fifty dollars raised in cash and seventy-five in pledges, leaving a balance due of seventy-five dollars on the church. 'Yours in gospel bonds, Elisha Weaver.'

articles.headline: The Presiding Eldership (from a Methodist Episcopal itinerant), with the Editor's Remarks
articles.author: A. Kent, New Bedford, Dec. 12, 1855
articles.summary: 'Rev. J. P. Campbell:--The Rev. Mr. Turner of this city put into my hands your Recorder of the 3d instant, in which I see something that ought to be corrected. I am a stranger to you, and yet I have begun in my fifty-fifth year in the itinerancy of the M.E. church. I have known your society from the time of your first general conference in 1816, and was in Philadelphia at the time. I have an interest for the well-being of your society, and reflect with satisfaction upon my exertions, by which the site for your church in this city was saved.' Kent corrects the Recorder's history of presiding elders in the M.E. Church -- there never was a class of 'ruling elders' distinct from them -- reviewing the usage from 1784 to 1792 with 78 elders, and closes, 'Whether it would be best for you to have such an office in the A.M.E. church, you must determine among yourselves.' A postscript (signed A. K.) warns that censorious articles 'will do harm to your societies, by engendering an unkind and bitter spirit.' The editor's 'Remarks' answer Elder Kent from 'the History of the Discipline by Bishop Emory' and 'History of M.E. Church, vol. II, N. Bangs,' restating: 'We are opposed to the introduction of another order of ministers in the A.M.E. church, and shall most conscientiously and religiously use all lawful means in our power to prevent its creation and existence.'

articles.headline: On Bishop Nazrey's plan for the Book Concern (a dissent in part)
articles.author: W. R. Revels, New Orleans, La., January [1?]th, 1856
articles.summary: 'Mr. Editor:--In the 37th number of the Recorder, I noticed an Editorial in which you have written at some length upon the plan proposed by Bishop Nazrey for raising a Fund for the better support of our book concern. And after a careful perusal of the Bishop's plan, and also, of your remarks thereupon, I must ask respectfully to dissent in part from the views advanced by each.' Revels agrees a capital of $10,000 should be raised and that the money is among our people, but holds that to enact a law making it obligatory upon each preacher and lay member, with a penalty annexed, 'would be downright oppression, something to which I have ever felt an utter abhorrence,' and that the uncultivated state of a great majority of our people utterly forbids such a procedure. Against the editorial's apparent design to restrict the ministry to men of means, he cites Luke from the medical profession, Apollos, Elisha from the plough, Peter from his fishing net, and Matthew from the receipt of custom, and Paul's epistle 1 Cor. i. 26-27 -- 'has not God almost always seemed pleased to select a majority of his ministers from among the humble class?... some of the best men in our ranks have been made bankrupts by a train of misfortunes for which they are not responsible.' He proposes instead shares of stock from $50 to $100 (sums under $10 received as donations) and an efficient agent appointed at the next general conference to frame and solicit aid for the book concern and paper, so that 'our present small, though precious sheet will grow to mammoth size.' 'Yours for the advancement of the cause of our common Saviour, W. R. Revels. New Orleans, La., January 1[?]th, 1856.' (Signature and place verified from the page image.)

articles.headline: Letter from the Jamaica Correspondent of the Moravian: The Past and the Future of Jamaica
articles.author: J. H. Buchner, Fairfield, Jamaica, Mandeville P.O., December 12, 1855
articles.summary: 'Dear Brethren:--All the world knows, that the West Indian Islands have become, and are becoming the land of the sable race...' A long Moravian missionary letter on emancipated Jamaica -- black and coloured men in the House of Assembly, estates passing to negro small farmers, the disappearance of white labour -- with an excursion after Carib/Indian remains at Pedro Bluff and the death-bed of a national helper; followed by statistics of the missionary operations of the Moravian Church, hints for maintaining harmony in a family, verses by the late James Montgomery, and a squib on crime in California. Reprint matter, skimmed per rule; no A.M.E. or Philadelphia names.

events.name: Anniversary of the life and death of Rt. Rev. Richard Allen, Bethel Church
events.location: Bethel A.M.E. Church, Sixth street, Philadelphia
events.description: Reported in the March 4 issue (No. 39) by 'A Spectator.' Held 'on Thursday, 4th of February' as printed (Feb. 4, 1856 was in fact a Monday; Thursday fell on the 14th -- the printed date is recorded as it stands), with a very good attendance notwithstanding the intensity of the weather. On motion, Rev. Richard Robertson was made chairman and beautifully addressed the meeting; the Rev. William Mook [so printed; possibly Monk or Moore] was introduced and told the time and place of Richard Allen's birth -- 'though born a slave, yet through his own perseverance he rose to be one of the greatest men of his age... there is not one living in the present generation among the ministers of our Church surpasses an Allen' -- being interrupted by young men in the gallery rushing to the street at the sound of passing music ('I say that we should love music in its right place'). After an ineffectual attempt by the choir to sing a hymn, three young misses attached to the Sunday School delivered a very short but interesting oration. Then the Rev. Dr. J. J. G. Bias, 'in his usual, peculiar, and eccentric manner, succeeded in riveting the attention of the audience on him for the space of sixty minutes': he regretted that his colleague Rev. J. P. Campbell was not present according to promise; recounted Father Allen's exodus from the pro-slavery M.E. Church, his hunting up the poor people through the lanes and alleys, the first church of the kind on Fifth St., his surrender of it ('we will not quarrel, but take the building for an Episcopal Church. What we want is an African Methodist Episcopal Church'), his blacksmith shop removed to Sixth St. for the friends to worship in until the present church was built; called Allen 'a thorough anti-slavery man... the most influential person that was among our people'; warned that some members of the general conference would purchase the discipline of the M.E. Church rather than revise their own ('I will take a stone, and go on the commons, and worship it, rather than be identified with such a class'); and invoked the slave mother now in Cincinnati, Margaret Gardner [Garner], who preferred to draw the knife across the throat of her innocent babe rather than have it returned to slavery -- 'her name shall go from generation to generation.' The concluding remarks were made by the Rev. Mr. Robertson, after which the benediction was pronounced.
attendees: chairman of the meeting; opening and concluding addresses
speaker on Allen's life (surname as printed; possibly Monk or Moore -- microfilm type unclear)
Rev. Dr. J. J. G. Bias
principal address, sixty minutes, on Allen, the M.E. discipline men, and Margaret Garner

events.name: Dedication of the A.M.E. church in Chicago
events.description: From Elisha Weaver's letter in the March 4 issue. 'The dedication of the A.M.E. church took place on the 6th of January, 1856, at half past two o'clock, P.M., conducted by the Rt. Rev. D. A. Payne, Bishop, and assisted by Elisha Weaver, the Minister, and Rev. John A. Warren, of the Ohio Conference, and Rev. H. C. Young, of the Canada Conference.' The bishop and ministers were met by the trustees at the door of the west aisle, moving in procession up the aisle reading the 84th Psalm responsively; the choir, led by Mr. C. H. Campbell, sung the anthem 'I was glad when they said unto me' from the Lute of Zion; Bishop Payne preached from the 27th Psalm, 4th and 6th verses -- 'upon the whole, it was theological in every minutia.' A crowded house, good order and decorum; in relation to contributions, 'we had those noble-hearted gentlemen, Mr. Lunt and Mr. Waughty, to lead off with their twenty-five dollars and twenty dollars, in connexion with a number of other gentlemen and ladies.' Amount raised in cash one hundred and fifty dollars, with pledges of seventy-five dollars, leaving a balance due of seventy-five dollars on the church (the first house was built some 12 or 14 years ago; the land is now worth some $1,200). Service was closed by Rev. Joseph H. Leonard, pastor of the Seamen's Bethel church of this city, singing the hymn. All names verified against the page image ('Mr. Waughty' remains slightly uncertain in the type).

events.name: Second quarterly meeting and revival at Zanesville, Ohio
events.description: From A. R. Green's letter of Jan. 31, 1856 (March 4 issue). 'Our second quarterly meeting was on the 13th inst.'; after Monday night's love feast Green announced the continuance of the meeting, advised the professors of religion to unite for a revival, and two young men and a woman voluntarily came forward; the protracted meeting was still going on at this writing. 'Twenty-four have professed the new birth, and some seven or eight happily reclaimed, and the whole church revived. Among the converts is my little daughter.' The house was crowded every evening, 'both white and black are bowing; four of our white friends have also found pardon'; 'our M.E. brethren are labouring faithfully with us, and our Baptist brethren are coming up to the help of the Lord.'
attendees: preacher in charge at Zanesville; author of the report (his little daughter among the converts)

events.name: Reception of Thos. Sunrise by the New England Annual Conference
events.description: Recounted in Thos. Sunrise's letter (Jan. 18 issue): 'the New England Annual Conference, held in Providence, R.I., June 16th, received me. They received me for two years' probation, the Bishop deciding that I be taken up by the church, and appointed me as a missionary... the Conference only gave me five dollars for my year's support.' Sunrise, an Indian and not of African descent, had applied to join the connexion some seven or eight years earlier under the charge of Thomas Lawrence, in Pittsburgh, Pa., and was then refused because the constitution and discipline did not allow receiving persons who were not descendants of Africans. (Year of the Providence session not printed; June 16 [1855] from context.)
attendees: Indian preacher received on two years' probation and appointed missionary
